passage: Your chechi Binita was fifteen when she got that photo app, mone. Your grandpa Jomon watched it all. Every night she would lie on the sofa scrolling other girls' holidays and perfect skin, and her face would go flat. If a photo got fewer hearts than her friend's, she deleted it. One evening she said, "Appachan, everyone's life is better than mine." I didn't lecture her. I just asked her to help with the church choir's Christmas concert, since she sings well. She came to practice every week. On the night she sang the solo, and her school friends came and shouted her name. After that I noticed she scrolled less. She'd say, "Can't, practice."

qa.q: What would Binita do if a photo got fewer hearts than her friend's?
What does Binita's flat face while scrolling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt low and behind, comparing herself with other girls' holidays and perfect skin.

qa.q: What turning point did the choir concert bring?
qa.a: Singing the solo with her real friends cheering gave her worth she could feel offline, and after that she scrolled less.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Binita said everyone's life was better than hers?
qa.a: He was probably worried and sad, which is why he looked for something real she could shine at instead of lecturing.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a fifteen-year-old whose mood rose and fell with likes, and how singing with friends gave her firmer ground.

passage: The school trek to Kalsubai had one bar of signal, Omkar's battery was at nine percent, and he was panicking. He'd posted a gym photo that morning and it had only fourteen likes. Aparna's post had two hundred. "Everyone thinks I'm a joke," he muttered, holding the phone up to the grey sky. "Your phone's going to die anyway," Aparna said, pulling up her hood. "Help me with the tent?" The phone died at the second pole. They got the tent up in the drizzle, badly, then properly, laughing when it collapsed on Aparna. That night by the lantern, their teacher said theirs was the best-pitched tent in the group. Omkar realised he hadn't thought about the likes in hours.

qa.q: How many likes did Omkar's gym photo get?
What was Omkar feeling when he held the phone up to the sky, and why?
qa.a: He felt anxious and embarrassed, thinking everyone saw him as a joke because his post had fewer likes than Aparna's.

qa.q: What turning point came once the phone died?
qa.a: He joined Aparna in pitching the tent, and the shared effort and the teacher's praise gave him firmer ground than likes.

qa.q: How might Aparna have seen Omkar's worry about likes?
qa.a: She seemed to see it as less important than what was in front of them, and gently pulled him into doing something together.

grounding: On a trek with a dying phone, a teenager who measures himself by likes finds firmer ground in a shared task and a friend.
